    AI Overview
    +11
    Psychedelic drugs are a class of psychoactive substances that profoundly alter perception, thought, and feeling, often inducing hallucinations and intense emotional experiences known as "trips". They primarily work by affecting serotonin receptors in the brain, changing how different brain regions communicate. Common types include LSD, psilocybin ("magic mushrooms"), and DMT. 
    Key Characteristics and Effects 
    • Altered Reality: Users may experience sensory blending (e.g., "hearing colors"), altered time perception, and intense, vivid hallucinations.
    • "Set and Setting": Effects are highly dependent on the user's mindset ("set") and environment ("setting")
      .
    • Physical Effects: Common reactions include dilated pupils, increased heart rate, and sometimes nausea.
    • Low Addiction Potential: Generally, classical psychedelics are not considered addictive. 
    Common Types of Psychedelics 
    • LSD (Lysergic acid diethylamide): A synthetic compound derived from a fungus, often taken on blotter paper.
    • Psilocybin (Magic Mushrooms): Naturally occurring mushrooms.
    • Mescaline (Peyote): Derived from a cactus.
    • DMT (N,N-Dimethyltryptamine): A potent, fast-acting compound found in various plants and animals.
    • Ayahuasca: A psychoactive brew containing DMT and other ingredients. 
    Risks and Therapeutic Potential 
    • Risks: "Bad trips" can cause extreme panic, paranoia, and terrifying hallucinations. In rare cases, they can trigger long-term mental health issues.
    • Therapeutic Use: Emerging research indicates that substances like psilocybin and LSD have potential for treating depression, anxiety, and PTSD.
    • Legal Status: In the U.S. and many other places, these are largely classified as Schedule 1 drugs, meaning they are considered to have high abuse potential and no accepted medical use, though this is evolving with new research. 
    Other Substance Classifications
    While often grouped together, other substances have different effects: 
    • Dissociatives: Compounds like ketamine and PCP (phencyclidine) can cause a feeling of being detached from one's body.
    • Entactogens: Substances like MDMA (ecstasy) focus more on emotional connection and empathy. 
    Disclaimer: Psychedelic drugs are illegal in most jurisdictions, and their use carries significant legal and safety risks.
